human_tolerance.notes: 'Fox squirrels are tolerant of human proximity, and even thrive in crowded urban and suburban environments. They exploit human habitations for sources of food and nesting sites, being as happy nesting in an attic as they are in a hollow tree.' Most often found in forest patches of 40 hectares or less with an open understory, 'or in urban neighborhoods with trees'.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: First estrus: 'Female fox squirrels come into estrus in mid-December or early January, then again in June.' Males give high-pitched whines during mating.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: Second estrus in June. Females normally produce two litters a year, though yearling females may only produce one.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Gestation 44-45 days. Earliest litters appear in late January; most births occur in mid-March and July; average litter size is three. Young are born blind, without fur and helpless; eyes open at 4-5 weeks and ears at 6 weeks; weaned between 12 and 14 weeks and not self-supporting until 16 weeks. Juveniles usually disperse in September or October, and may den together or with their mother through their first winter.

phases.name: caching
phases.note: 'Fox squirrels will form caches by burying food items for later consumption. They like to store foods that are shelled and high in fat, such as acorns and nuts.'

phases.name: dormancy
phases.note: 'Tree dens are preferred over leaf nests during the winter'; winter dens are hollows in tree trunks, sometimes worn out by 'a succession of occupants over as many as 30 years', and shared by breeding pairs. The source describes winter den use rather than true hibernation, so the phase marks the denning season.

vocalizations.description: 'The most common vocalization for fox squirrels is a series of barks.' They also 'warn of approaching threats with distress screams' and give tooth chatters and breathy barks as indications of stress; in spring and autumn, groups clucking and chucking together can make a small ruckus.

'They also make high-pitched whines during mating. When threatening another fox squirrel, they will stand upright with their tail over their back and flick it.' Grunts and squeals are given by restrained animals and during male-male chase.

external.note: GBIF usage key, authorship and order from the GBIF Backbone Taxonomy; the iNaturalist taxa API matched taxon 46020 to 'Eastern Fox Squirrel'; ITIS TSN and NCBI taxon id from Wikidata (P815, P685). The Wikidata item sits at the title 'Fox squirrel', which is the current name of the English Wikipedia article; 'eastern fox squirrel' and 'Bryant's fox squirrel' are listed there as synonyms.

common_names.note: 'The fox squirrel (Sciurus niger), also known as the eastern fox squirrel or Bryant's fox squirrel'. The record uses 'Eastern fox squirrel', the name the Colorado locale's issue and current bird-trade usage prefer; the Wikipedia article title is 'Fox squirrel'.

conservation.note: Wikidata P141 = least concern. Wikipedia adds that 'because of overhunting and the destruction of mature forests, many subspecies of fox squirrel are endangered' - a subspecies-level statement that does not alter the species-level status.

range.note: 'The fox squirrel's natural range extends through most of the eastern United States, north into the southern prairie provinces of Canada, west to the Dakotas, Colorado, and Texas, and south to the northern parts of Coahuila, Nuevo Leon... and Tamaulipas. It is absent (except for vagrants) in New England, New Jersey, most of New York, northern and eastern Pennsylvania, Ontario, Quebec, and the Atlantic provinces of Canada. It has been introduced to both northern and southern California, Oregon, Idaho, Montana, Washington, New Mexico, and Utah, as well as Ontario and British Columbia in Canada.' US-CO is therefore listed as native on the strength of the source. NOTE: the issue that prompted this locale stated that eastern fox squirrels are introduced in Colorado; that contradicts the source, which lists Colorado inside the natural range, and the source is followed here. The state list is an approximation of 'most of the eastern United States' plus the named plains states and is not exhaustive; no elevation range is given, so elevation_m is omitted.

traits.note: Covers the structural traits (body plan, limb count, thermoregulation, skin, flight, respiration, metamorphosis) and locomotion modes: 'spend more of their time on the ground than most other tree squirrels. They are still, however, agile climbers', with 'sharp claws, developed extensors of digits and flexors of forearms, and abdominal musculature' for climbing, and 'impressive jumpers, easily spanning 15 feet in horizontal leaps' - the horizontal bound is carried by the Gallop mode, which the quadruped body plan can animate. Individual numeric and behavioural traits below carry their own entries.

traits.nest_type.note: 'They construct two types of homes called "dreys"... Summer dreys are often little more than platforms of sticks high in the branches of trees, while winter dens are usually hollowed out of tree trunks', and 'they generally use natural cavities or cavities created by northern flickers (Colaptes auratus) or red-headed woodpeckers'. The winter den and nursery in a tree cavity are the record's nest type; the summer drey is carried in habitat.resources as nest_platform.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (~0.79 kg); the validator's size-class bands place this in the Small band, though the animal is 'the largest species of tree squirrel native to North America'.

traits.mass_kg.note: Midpoint of the stated 1.0-2.5 lb range (453.6-1,134.0 g), 793.8 g. 'There is no sexual dimorphism in size or appearance. Individuals tend to be smaller in the West.'

traits.mass_range_kg.note: Stated range 1.0-2.5 lb, converted to 453.6-1,134.0 g.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of the stated total length 20-30 in (50.8-76.2 cm), as the schema asks for nose to tail tip. The source also gives a body length of 10-15 in (25.4-38.1 cm) with a similar tail length, which is what the mesh proportions are set from.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'Their maximum life expectancy is typically 12.6 years for females and 8.6 years for males', against 'in captivity, fox squirrels have been known to live about 18 years' and the reproductive longevity of 'over 12 years'. The mean of the two sex-specific maxima, 10.6 years, is used; the source gives no typical (as opposed to maximum) wild lifespan, so this is an upper-central figure.

traits.diet.note: Diet section: 'Food habits of fox squirrels depend largely on geographic location. In general, fox squirrel foods include mast, tree buds, insects, tubers, bulbs, roots, bird eggs, pine nuts and spring-fruiting trees, and fungi. Agricultural crops such as corn, soybeans, oats, wheat, and fruit are also eaten.' Shares follow that ordering with mast dominant - 'they thrive among oak, hickory, walnut, pecan and pine trees, storing their nuts for winter' - browse (tree buds and twigs) and invertebrates next, and crops as seed. No sourced percentages were found, so the numbers are judgement.

traits.social.note: 'Fox squirrels are not particularly gregarious or playful; in fact, they have been described as solitary and asocial creatures, coming together only in breeding season', with cohabitation of a winter den 'particularly among breeding pairs'.

traits.defense.note: Judgement: they give distress screams and tooth-chatter at stress, and stand upright with the tail over the back to threaten another squirrel, but the shared ground-forager program responds to a close threat by moving away, and adult escape is by running and leaping, so Flee was authored.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: 'Fox squirrels are tolerant of human proximity, and even thrive in crowded urban and suburban environments', so a low wariness value was authored.

habitat.note: Covers shelter_tag and habitat.resources. Food tags come from the Diet section; cavity and nest_platform from the two shelter types (tree dens and leaf dreys) in the Distribution and habitat and Behavior sections. Weights are judgement, not separately sourced percentages.

habitat.use.note: 'spend more of their time on the ground than most other tree squirrels. They are still, however, agile climbers'; 'Fox squirrels are often observed foraging on the ground several hundred meters from the nearest woodlot', and they use tree canopies, forks and dens for shelter and breeding.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Distribution and habitat section: 'Fox squirrels are tolerant of human proximity, and even thrive in crowded urban and suburban environments. They exploit human habitations for sources of food and nesting sites, being as happy nesting in an attic as they are in a hollow tree', and 'most often found... in urban neighborhoods with trees'.

seasonal.strategy.note: The source describes no migration and states the species is 'strictly diurnal' with year-round den use and winter food caching, so ActiveYearRound was used.

seasonal.phases.note: Two oestrus periods (mid-December to early January, and June), two litters with the quoted gestation, birth timing and litter size, the juvenile development schedule, autumn cache-building and winter denning. Day-of-month boundaries other than 'mid-December', 'late January' and 'mid-March' are judgement. The phase named dormancy marks the winter denning season described in the source rather than true hibernation, and carries a fraction because dens are shared by breeding pairs and not every animal is in one all winter; that fraction is judgement.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Reproduction section: 'At birth, the young are blind, without fur, and helpless. Their eyes open at 4 to 5 weeks and their ears open at 6 weeks. Fox squirrels are weaned between 12 and 14 weeks, but may not be self-supporting until 16 weeks. Juveniles usually disperse in September or October, but may den either together or with their mother during their first winter.' duration_days 252 is derived from those 12-16 weeks (midpoint about 15 weeks plus the autumn dispersal period) and scale 0.55 is judgement for a young animal; the requires_tag records that a den must be present.

vocalizations.bark.note: Vocalization and Behavior sections: 'The most common vocalization for fox squirrels is a series of barks', with 'distress screams' as the threat warning and 'tooth chatters and breathy barks... indications of stress'.

vocalizations.mating_whine.note: Behavior section: 'They also make high-pitched whines during mating. When threatening another fox squirrel, they will stand upright with their tail over their back and flick it.' season_months follows the two oestrus periods in the source. The id carries an underscore because the validator restricts call ids to lowercase letters, digits and underscores.

look.note: Description section: 'In most areas, the animal's upper body is brown-grey to brown-yellow with a typically brownish-orange underside, while in eastern regions, such as the Appalachians, there are more strikingly-patterned dark brown and black squirrels with white bands on the face and tail. In the South and parts of Nebraska and Iowa along the Missouri River, there are populations with uniform black coats.' The palette takes the western brown-grey to brown-yellow morph that Colorado falls in, with the brownish-orange underside on the belly slot; the tail_fluff extra part matches the record's own tail, keeping the plume visible as the tail moves. Proportions are authored judgement, set from the 25.4-38.1 cm body length and similar tail length.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared ground-forager program: food_tag is mast, the dominant diet share and what the program uses for foraging; flee_m and calm_m are judgement for an animal that tolerates people but flees fast and leaps; flee_gait gallop matches the 15-foot horizontal leaps, forage_gait walk matches the slow ground foraging 'several hundred meters from the nearest woodlot'; rest_sun_lo/hi set the rest window to night, since the species is strictly diurnal.
